Kalash Quality Systems: The Accounts That Looked Fine

Hyderabad, September 2026. Nandita Rao has nineteen days to tell her board which customers will not renew — and the number she has been using has been wrong five times out of seven.

1. Nineteen days

On the evening of 17 September 2026, in Kalash Quality Systems' office in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, Nandita Rao printed a single sheet of paper and laid it beside her keyboard. It listed the seven customers Kalash had lost in the previous eight months. Against each, in a column her customer-success team had not expected anyone to audit, was the health score the company's dashboard had shown ninety days before the loss. Five of the seven read green.

Nandita, thirty-eight, had joined Kalash as head of product two years earlier after nine years in regulated-industry software. On 6 October she would present the renewal outlook for the January–March season to the board, including the chairman and two investor directors. Of Kalash's ₹38 crore of annual recurring revenue, ₹16.4 crore came up for renewal in that quarter. The board would want to know how much of it was safe. Nandita had concluded that she did not currently possess an honest way to answer.

2. The company

Kalash sold an electronic quality management system to regulated manufacturers: document and SOP control, deviation logging, corrective and preventive action workflows, change control, training records, supplier qualification and electronic batch release. Its customers were mid-sized Indian pharmaceutical formulation companies, contract manufacturers and, increasingly, food processors — 214 accounts at an average of ₹17.8 lakh a year, plus eleven large accounts above ₹60 lakh.

The company had been founded in 2017 by two former quality heads from Hyderabad's pharmaceutical belt who had spent their careers preparing sites for inspection. Their timing was fortunate. The revised Schedule M of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules pushed Indian manufacturers towards documented, auditable quality systems on a phased timetable, and firms exporting to the United States had long needed records that satisfied 21 CFR Part 11. Food customers arrived later, driven by FSSAI audit requirements and by the documentation that large buyers such as organised retail chains demanded of their suppliers. Kalash competed at the low end against spreadsheets and paper, in the middle against internally built systems on Zoho Creator, and at the top against global eQMS vendors whose licences ran three to five times its price. Its pitch was unfussy: inspection-ready records at Indian pricing, with a Hyderabad-based team that had themselves faced a CDSCO inspector across a table.

The team was distributed, as Indian B2B software teams now routinely are. Engineering sat in Hyderabad and Pune; the design lead worked from Berlin; the data scientist was in Toronto; customer success was run from Singapore, which covered India, South-East Asia and the Gulf within one working day; and a four-person sales team in Edison, New Jersey, sold to Indian-owned generics manufacturers with United States operations. The single largest account, at ₹1.9 crore, was Qudra Pharma FZ-LLC, a Dubai-based generics exporter with plants in Gujarat and Ras Al Khaimah.

3. The situation

Kalash's health score had been built eighteen months earlier by Shalini Iyer, the VP of customer success in Singapore, in a fortnight, out of what was available: sixty per cent weighted on monthly active users as a share of licensed seats, twenty-five per cent on an inverted support-ticket count, and fifteen per cent on a satisfaction rating that customer-success managers entered after each quarterly review. It was legible, it fitted on a slide, and it had been adopted everywhere — in board packs, in the sales forecast, and in the bonus structure for the customer-success team.

It also could not have worked. Kalash's product was, in its core module, compulsory: a manufacturer operating under a documented quality system must log deviations, and it logs them where its SOPs say it logs them. Across the whole book, monthly active users sat between 82 and 94 per cent of licensed seats, and the churned accounts sat inside that band along with everybody else. The variable carried almost no information. The ticket count was worse than uninformative: it fell to near zero in accounts that had quietly stopped using anything beyond the mandatory module, and the score read that silence as contentment.

When Nandita went back through the seven losses, a different pattern was visible without any modelling at all. Six of the seven had bought four or more modules and had fewer than two live. Five had not put a single supplier qualification record into the system in six months. Four had lost the quality head who signed the original contract. And in the three cases where Kalash's own implementation team had a record of it, none of the seven had used Kalash during their most recent regulatory audit; they had exported records into spreadsheets and worked from those, which is the clearest possible statement that the system was not trusted where it mattered most.

Seen from Singapore, the problem was capacity. Shalini's team of six covered 214 accounts. Seen from Toronto, the problem was that nobody had ever fitted a model. Seen from New Jersey, the problem was that a re-scored book would turn several accounts amber a fortnight before the quarter closed. Seen from Pune, the problem was that the module-level usage events Nandita wanted to score on had been instrumented in 2023, never validated, and were missing entirely for the nine customers on on-premise installations — including two of the eleven largest.

4. The people

Shalini Iyer, VP customer success, Singapore, had built the existing score and defended it without embarrassment: it had been the best thing possible in a fortnight with no instrumentation. What she wanted now was a licensed customer-success platform at about ₹24 lakh a year, which would give her workflows, playbooks and an out-of-the-box health model in six weeks. Her team's retention bonus was calculated on the share of ARR in green accounts.

Priya Menon, senior data scientist, Toronto, wanted to fit a proper churn model on account-quarters. She had run the numbers on feasibility and been candid about the limitation: Kalash had thirty-one churn events across three years, which she described in a Slack message at 02:10 India time as "enough to check a story, not enough to learn one."

Vikram Sethi, head of sales, Edison, New Jersey, had two of his largest United States-facing accounts in the January cohort and was frank that a sudden repainting of the book would be read by the board as a product failure rather than a measurement correction. He also had the most useful single observation anyone offered: in his experience, an account that declined a joint audit rehearsal had already decided.

Kaushik Barve, engineering lead, Pune, owned the instrumentation. He estimated three weeks to validate module-level usage events and a further four to build a nightly rollup by account and site. For the nine on-premise customers he could offer nothing without a contract amendment permitting log export — a live question under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, since deviation records contain named employees.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Renewal outcome by health band, eight quarters to August 2026

All2193,73019790%

Source: Kalash CRM renewal records joined to dashboard snapshots taken ninety days before each renewal date. Note that eleven of the twenty-two losses came from the green band, which held 77 per cent of accounts.

Exhibit 1 is the heart of Nandita's problem. A health score earns its bands by showing that accounts in different bands behave differently. Here, green renews at 92 per cent and red at 75 per cent against a book average of 90 — a separation so weak that knowing an account's colour barely changes what one should expect. Worse, because the green band is so large, it contains half the losses in absolute terms. The score was not lying; it was merely almost silent, and silence dressed in colour is read as reassurance.

Read across Exhibit 2 rather than down it. Monthly active users, the variable carrying sixty per cent of the score's weight, ranges from 58 to 91 per cent and tells almost nothing. The breadth column tells a great deal: six of seven accounts had bought between three and six modules and were running one or two. The sponsor column and the audit column, neither of which entered the score at all, are the two that would have flagged the largest losses months in advance. Nandita noted that the audit column was incomplete — a fact she would have to state plainly to the board rather than quietly drop.

Exhibit 3 — What each option costs, and what it buys

6. The options

Option A: licence a customer-success platform. Shalini's preference. It arrives quickly, brings playbooks and task management her team badly needs, and gives the board a recognisable name to hear. The cost is ₹24 lakh a year and, more seriously, the fact that its default health model is assembled from logins, tickets and survey responses — exactly the three families of signal that Exhibit 1 shows to be nearly silent in Kalash's business. The platform would make the existing failure faster and better organised.

Option B: fit a churn model. Priya's preference, and intellectually the most satisfying. Thirty-one events across three years is thin, and the model could not be validated before the January renewals; it would also be blind to the nine on-premise accounts and to the sponsor and audit signals, which live in the CRM and in implementation notes rather than in the product. It is the right destination and the wrong vehicle for nineteen days.

Option C: build a three-component rubric score and back-test it. Depth as records created per licensed site against the account's own trailing median; breadth as modules live over modules sold, and sites live over sites contracted; engagement as a four-item checklist — named sponsor met in the last two quarters, certified administrator in post, audit rehearsal accepted, invoices current. Weights set by judgement, published, and tested against the thirty-one known outcomes. It is ready in three weeks, covers on-premise accounts through manual entry for nine customers, and can be explained to a CSM. It is also, undeniably, a set of opinions rather than a fitted model.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1 alone, what would you conclude about the existing score, and what exactly should Nandita say about it to the board on 6 October?

2. Exhibit 2 contains one column that is incomplete and one variable that carries most of the score's weight while explaining nothing. Which signals would you keep, which would you drop, and what would you add that Kalash does not currently collect?

3. Shalini's team is paid on the share of ARR in green accounts. How does that fact change the design of any score Nandita builds, and what would you do about it?

4. Which option should Nandita choose, and what would you commit to doing by 6 October, by mid-November and by the end of March?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a single idea: a health score is a standing bet on which accounts will not renew, and it is worth exactly what its record of settling that bet says it is worth. Exhibit 1 is that record. Once a learner reads it correctly — bands that do not separate outcomes, and a green band so wide that it contains most of the losses — most of the apparent complexity dissolves. The question is not whether to have a score but which signals carry information about this product in this market.

The structural insight is that in a regulated product, usage is partly compulsory, and compulsory usage cannot discriminate. Everybody logs deviations because Schedule M and the customer's own SOPs require it. What varies, and therefore what predicts, is breadth — how much of what was sold is actually switched on — and engagement — whether a sponsor exists and whether the customer trusts the system when an inspector is in the building. Exhibit 2 shows both signals sitting in plain view outside the score.

A defensible path runs roughly as follows. Take Option C now, and be explicit that it is a rubric, not a forecast. Set the weights by judgement — depth 0.30, breadth 0.45, engagement 0.25 — back-test them on the thirty-one known outcomes, publish the resulting band-by-band renewal rates alongside Exhibit 1's, and let the comparison make the argument. Cut the red band at whatever score gives Shalini's six people about twenty-five accounts, because a red list longer than the team can work is not a priority list. Move the CSM sentiment field out of the arithmetic and display it beside the score as a visible, auditable override, which protects the number from the bonus scheme without discarding what CSMs genuinely know. Fund Kaushik's three weeks of instrumentation validation regardless of the option chosen, because every path depends on it. Commit to Priya's fitted model for the following financial year, by which point the instrumentation will have produced clean account-quarters and the event count will have roughly doubled. And tell the board the uncomfortable part directly: five of seven losses were green, the audit column is missing for three accounts, and the January forecast will be presented as a range with its assumptions stated.

Reasonable people could argue for buying the platform as well, on the grounds that Shalini's team needs workflow tooling whatever the score says — that is a defensible amendment, provided the platform's default health model is switched off rather than adopted. What is not defensible is presenting the January outlook on 6 October using a number that has already been shown, on the company's own evidence, to be nearly silent.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Account Health Scores

Which accounts are at risk before they tell us?

1. A Tuesday in August, Bengaluru

On the morning of 4 August 2026, Meera Iyer, VP of Customer Success at Lohit Systems, was rereading a churn notice that still did not make sense to her. Hind Carriers, a 90-truck fleet operator in Nagpur, had been a customer of Lohit FleetOS — the company's trip-planning and driver-compliance platform for mid-market logistics fleets — for two years. Its account had shown a Net Promoter Score of 9 at the last survey, no open support escalations, and a renewal booked for October at ₹22 lakh in annual recurring revenue. Three weeks ago, Hind Carriers's owner had signed with a competitor instead, citing a "loss of confidence" that nobody at Lohit had seen coming.

Meera's team ran eleven customer success managers across four cities, covering 340 accounts and roughly ₹61 crore of ARR. Renewal season for the next quarter was about to open, with 58 accounts up for renewal representing ₹14.2 crore. If even a handful of those looked like Hind Carriers — quiet, technically satisfied, and quietly gone — the team would find out only when the notice arrived. Kabir Saxena, who led analytics for customer success from Hyderabad, had spent the past month building a composite account health score meant to prevent exactly this. Ritu Deshpande, who ran renewals out of Pune, wanted to trust it enough to prioritise her outreach calls around it. Meera's decision, ahead of a leadership review that Friday, was whether the score was ready to guide 58 renewal conversations, or whether it would simply give the team a confident, wrong number instead of an honest, uncertain one.

2. The idea

An account health score is a single composite number, built from a small set of observable account behaviours, that estimates how likely a given customer is to renew, expand, or churn within a defined window. It was invented to solve a specific problem created by the shift to subscription software: in a perpetual-licence world, a customer who was unhappy still had a sunk cost that kept them around; in a subscription world, unhappiness converts directly into a lost renewal, often with almost no warning, because the customer's exit costs a single decision not to sign again. As SaaS matured through the 2000s and 2010s and customer success became its own discipline — distinct from support, which reacts, and from sales, which closes — practitioners needed a leading indicator that did not depend on customers volunteering how they felt, since by the time they volunteered it, the decision was often already made.

The sentence Meera could repeat in Friday's review without sounding glib is this: a health score turns scattered signals of usage, breadth, and engagement into one number so the team can act while there is still time to change the outcome, rather than explain the outcome after the fact.

3. How it actually works

Building a defensible health score is a sequence of choices, and the steps practitioners most often skip are the validation ones, not the arithmetic ones. First comes the objective: what, exactly, is the score predicting, and over what window? Kabir defined Lohit's score to predict non-renewal within the customer's next 90-day renewal window — a specific, falsifiable target, rather than a vague "is this account healthy."

Second comes selecting candidate inputs, grouped into families rather than a long flat list: usage depth (how intensively the licensed seats are actually used), breadth of adoption (how many of the product's modules have moved from "enabled" to "habitually used"), and engagement or relationship signals (sentiment, support load, and continuity of the customer's internal champion). Third, and the step most teams shortcut, is backtesting each candidate input against accounts that have already churned or renewed, to check that it actually separates the two groups before it is trusted with a weight. Kabir pulled eighteen months of account history and found that weekly active users as a share of licensed seats separated churned from renewed accounts cleanly, while raw login counts did not — a handful of churned accounts had inflated login counts from a single frustrated user checking the product obsessively before leaving.

Fourth, each surviving input is normalised onto a common 0–100 scale, since raw units cannot be combined — "weekly active users" and "days since last executive contact" have no shared arithmetic. Fifth, weights are assigned to each family, ideally set by regressing historical churn against the normalised inputs rather than by a workshop vote, though early on a defensible manual weighting, revisited quarterly, is an honest substitute. Sixth, the weighted inputs are summed into a composite score and bucketed — commonly red, amber, green — against thresholds chosen so the buckets actually predict different renewal rates, not thresholds chosen because they look tidy. Seventh, and this is the step that turns a spreadsheet into a working programme, every score needs an owner, a cadence, and a specified action: who looks at it, how often, and what they are supposed to do when it moves. A score nobody is accountable for acting on is decoration.

4. A worked example: Girivan Logistics

Girivan Logistics, a 140-truck fleet operator in Coimbatore, had been on Lohit FleetOS for fourteen months, paying ₹18 lakh a year, with twelve licensed seats across dispatch and compliance. Kabir's model scored the account as follows, using the 40/30/30 weighting from the diagram above.

InputRawNormalised (0–100)WeightContribution
Usage depth: weekly active users / 12 seats9 / 12750.4030.0
Breadth: modules used >1×/week of 5 enabled3 / 5600.3018.0
Engagement (before): avg of NPS 8/10→80, ticket health 80, sponsor continuity 100avg(80,80,100)870.3026.1
Composite score, before74.1 → 74 Green

Seventy-four crossed comfortably into green. Then, in late July, Girivan's operations head — the internal champion who had pushed the FleetOS rollout — left the company for a competitor fleet operator. Usage and module adoption had not yet moved; a departing champion shows up first in the engagement family, not in usage logs, which is precisely why engagement needs its own weighted input rather than being inferred from login counts. Sponsor continuity dropped from 100 to 0, pulling the engagement sub-score from 87 to an average of (80, 80, 0) = 53.

The ten-point drop moved Girivan from green to amber a full nine weeks before its renewal date — the exact warning Hind Carriers never gave, because Hind Carriers's champion turnover had never been captured as an input at all. The arithmetic is simple; the discipline is in choosing, in advance, which inputs actually carry that kind of signal.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

It predicts; it does not diagnose

A score of 64 tells Ritu that Girivan is at elevated risk. It does not tell her why in enough detail to act — that still requires a human call. Treating the score as an explanation rather than a trigger for one is the single most common misuse of the tool.

Weights must be earned, not assumed

The 40/30/30 split at Lohit came from regressing prior churn against candidate inputs; a workshop's intuition about what "feels important" routinely gets the weighting backwards, especially by over-weighting usage, which is easy to measure, and under-weighting relationship continuity, which is not.

Segments have different scores for a reason

Enterprise fleet accounts like Girivan churn on relationship and procurement events; small single-branch operators churn on price and simple neglect. A single national weighting scheme blurs both signals; Lohit eventually ran two weighting sets, one per segment.

Green accounts still churn

Acquisitions, budget freezes, and a rival's aggressive discount sit entirely outside any usage-based model. A health score narrows the set of surprises; it never eliminates them, and a team that promises otherwise will be embarrassed by exactly one exogenous event.

New accounts lack history to score fairly

An account three weeks into onboarding has no meaningful usage baseline yet; scoring it on the same curve as a two-year account either falsely flags normal ramp-up as risk or falsely reassures on too little data. Most mature programmes exclude, or separately score, anything under ninety days old.

Inputs can be gamed, deliberately or not

Once customer success managers know logins count toward the score, some nudge customers to click in without doing meaningful work, inflating the number while the underlying relationship keeps decaying. Choosing inputs that are hard to game cheaply — module breadth over raw logins — matters more than choosing inputs that are easy to collect.

Stale data makes the score lag reality

If engagement inputs refresh monthly but renewal decisions happen weekly, the score is describing last month's account, not this week's. The refresh cadence has to match the cadence of the decisions it feeds, or it quietly becomes theatre.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

Consumer products rarely speak of "account health" in this vocabulary, because there is no named account or relationship to manage — the analogous work is retention-curve and engagement-cohort analysis at the user level, aggregated statistically rather than tracked one customer at a time. B2B products, where Lohit sits, are the natural home of the health score precisely because there are few enough named accounts, each large enough in ARR, that a human being can own each one's number and act on it individually. Marketplace products sit in between and complicate the picture further: a logistics marketplace connecting fleet owners to shippers needs two health scores, one for supply-side accounts and one for demand-side accounts, because the two sides churn for different reasons and a single blended score obscures both.

Company stage matters just as much as product type. An early-stage company with forty customers and eighteen months of history, as Lohit itself once was, does not have enough churned accounts to regress a defensible weighting; the honest approach is a small number of manually weighted inputs, reviewed by the founding team every quarter, openly labelled as provisional. A larger company with hundreds of accounts and several years of outcomes, which is where Lohit stood by 2026, can and should validate weights statistically, segment by account type, and treat the score as an input to a broader customer-success operating system rather than a standalone spreadsheet.

7. Common mistakes

All-green until the churn notice. Symptom: the dashboard shows a healthy portfolio right up until a renewal is lost. Underlying cause: inputs were chosen for ease of measurement, not for their proven separation between past renewals and past churns. Cheapest diagnostic: backtest the current weighting against the last four to eight quarters of known outcomes before trusting it going forward.

One scheme for every segment. Symptom: enterprise accounts and small accounts cluster at oddly similar scores despite obviously different renewal behaviour. Underlying cause: a single national weighting hides segment-specific churn drivers. Cheapest diagnostic: compare bucket distribution and actual renewal rate within each segment separately.

No owner, no action, no cadence. Symptom: the score exists, is occasionally screenshotted in a review, and nothing changes when it moves. Underlying cause: the score was built as an analytics exercise, not as an operating mechanism. Cheapest diagnostic: ask, for the last ten accounts that dropped a bucket, who was notified and what they did within a week.

8. What good looks like

Six months after the Hind Carriers loss, Lohit's health score covered every account older than ninety days, split into two weighting schemes for enterprise and small-fleet segments, refreshed weekly against the cadence Ritu's team actually worked to, and backtested every quarter against the prior quarter's real renewals. Every bucket change triggered a specific, logged action — a CSM call within five business days for an amber drop, an executive escalation within two for red — and Kabir reviewed false positives and false negatives from the previous quarter before recalibrating weights. The score was never presented as certainty; it was presented, honestly, as the best current estimate of where the team's limited attention would do the most good.

9. What Meera decided

Meera approved the score for Friday's review, but not as an oracle: she asked Ritu to prioritise outreach by bucket while still requiring a documented reason whenever a CSM overrode the score's recommendation, and she asked Kabir to publish the backtest numbers alongside every review so the team could see, quarter over quarter, whether the score was actually improving or merely feeling authoritative. Girivan Logistics's amber flag reached Ritu's desk nine weeks before renewal, giving her account manager time to rebuild the relationship with Girivan's new operations lead before the contract came up — the outcome the score existed to produce, and the one Hind Carriers had never gotten.

The next topic worth Meera's team's attention is how these scores connect to renewal, churn, and net revenue retention arithmetic directly — because a health score is only useful insofar as it moves those numbers, and measuring that link closes the loop the score itself cannot close. Two questions worth sitting with: if your own team's health score went all-green the week before an account left, what input was missing, and would you know it was missing before the account left, or only after?

— Reading page prepared for the ISB Product Management knowledge graph.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Account Health Scores

Which accounts are at risk before they tell us — and how much of that question a single number can honestly answer?

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 11 August 2026, Aparna Rege, Chief Customer Officer at Dastak Systems in Pune, sat with a list of eleven accounts that had left over four quarters. Dastak sold Dastak Edge, a claims-adjudication platform used by health insurers and third-party administrators; the median contract ran ₹29 lakh a year, and renewals were decided by a committee including a procurement head Dastak's customer success managers had never met. The post-mortems classified nine of the eleven departures as “no prior signal.” Aparna did not believe that. Her analytics lead, Vikram Nadig, in Hyderabad, had fitted a model on 410 account-quarters and come back with an uncomfortable number: it could concentrate half the churn into the riskiest fifth of the portfolio, yet even the riskiest accounts renewed more often than they left. Sneha Bhatt, who ran renewals from Gurugram with capacity for about sixty genuine save-plays a quarter, wanted one thing before the October cycle opened: which sixty accounts.

Three days later and 1,000 kilometres south, Rohan Pillai, Head of Growth Product at Elaan Cloud in Chennai, faced a superficially identical question of an entirely different shape. Elaan Cloud sold a self-serve collaboration product — Elaan Teams at the low end, Elaan Enterprise above it — to 3,100 paying workspaces generating ₹40 crore of recurring revenue, averaging ₹1.3 lakh each. Elaan had no customer success managers for the long tail; it had lifecycle emails, in-product nudges and a four-person pooled team in Kochi under Imran Qureshi. Tanvi Kulkarni, Elaan's data scientist in Bengaluru, had built a workspace health score with a respectable area under the ROC curve of 0.81, and in July it turned 340 workspaces red in a single week. Ninety-six per cent of them renewed. Rohan's decision was whether to fix the score or to stop having one.

The two decisions frame the argument of this page. A health score is not primarily a modelling problem. It is a question about whether a ranked list of accounts can change what an organisation does, and the modelling matters only to the extent that it can.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

An account health score is a composite, periodically refreshed estimate — a number, a bucket, or a ranked queue — of the probability that a named account will fail to renew, contract or churn within a stated forward window. Three words carry weight. Composite: it aggregates several behaviours rather than reporting one. Named account: the unit is a commercial relationship, not a user. Stated forward window: a score with no horizon cannot be validated, because you never know when it was supposed to have been right.

The instrument exists because subscription economics removed the cushion perpetual licensing provided. When a customer paid once and maintained annually, dissatisfaction leaked out slowly through lapsed maintenance and a stalled upgrade path. Under subscription it converts to a single binary decision on a known date, often taken by people the vendor has never spoken to. From the mid-2000s the customer success discipline emerged to manage that exposure, and with it a demand for a leading indicator that did not require the customer to volunteer anything — because by the time a customer volunteers dissatisfaction, the alternative has usually already been evaluated.

The chart is the whole justification for the instrument and the seed of the disagreement about it. Four schools contend; it is worth stating what each would and would not sign.

The actuarial school holds that a health score is a churn probability and nothing else, testable only by out-of-sample discrimination and calibration. It signs: a score whose risk deciles do not match observed churn rates is broken however much the field likes it. It will not sign: the score should be simple enough to reconstruct by hand. The operational school, which most commercial customer-success platforms encode, holds that the score is a coordination device for routing scarce attention. It signs: a transparent weighted score account managers act on beats a black box with better discrimination that nobody opens. It will not sign: weights must come from a regression. The value-realisation school, strongest in enterprise, holds that usage proxies the thing that matters — whether the customer got the outcome the purchase was justified by. It signs: an account using the product heavily and getting nothing from it is unhealthy. It will not sign: engagement telemetry is sufficient. The disaggregationists hold that composition itself is the error, and that a few separately owned signals with thresholds are strictly better. They sign: the moment you add usage to sentiment you cannot tell which lever to pull. They will not sign: executives need one number.

Aparna's organisation was implicitly actuarial and value-realisation; Rohan's, at ₹1.3 lakh a workspace, could only be operational or disaggregationist, because value realisation presumes a conversation Elaan could not afford to have.

3. Mechanics in depth

The arithmetic of a weighted score is trivial and is not where expertise lives. Expertise lives in six decisions that precede it, each with a second-order effect that surfaces a quarter later.

The label. Define the event predicted and its window. Vikram chose “fails to renew, or renews at under 80 per cent of prior ARR, within 90 days,” folding contraction into churn because Dastak's downgrades were commoner than departures and had the same causes. A subtler consequence: since contracts were annual, only accounts reaching a renewal date produced a label, which left-truncates the data and trains the model on survivors. The three accounts that died in onboarding never appear.

Feature selection under leakage discipline. Every candidate is tested for availability at the moment the score must be useful. “Customer requested a data export” predicts churn beautifully and is worthless: it arrives four days before the notice. Vikram made lead time a hard filter, dropping any feature whose median first movement fell under thirty days.

The model. Dastak fitted a logistic regression, chosen over a marginally better gradient-boosted tree because Sneha's team needed reason codes. It estimates the log-odds of the event as a linear sum, z = β0 + Σβixi, with probability p = 1 / (1 + e−z). The coefficients below come from 410 account-quarters containing 63 events, a base rate of 15.4 per cent.

FeatureβOdds ratioReading
Intercept−3.30—Baseline log-odds
Champion/sponsor changed in last 90 days+1.554.71Largest single effect
Active-seat ratio decline, per 10 pp+0.742.10Gradual, well-instrumented
Modules habitually used, per module−0.410.66Breadth protects
Open P1 escalation aged > 14 days+1.103.00Ageing, not volume
Executive-sponsor contact in last 60 days−0.520.59Confounded — see below
ln(ARR in ₹ lakh)−0.190.83Larger accounts stickier

Applied to Firoza Diagnostics, a ₹31 lakh account: sponsor changed (+1.55), active-seat ratio down 18 points (1.8 × 0.74 = +1.33), two modules habitual (−0.82), one P1 open nineteen days (+1.10), no executive contact (0), ln(31) × −0.19 = −0.65. With the intercept, z = −0.79, so p = 1/(1 + e0.79) = 0.31. Firoza was the second-riskiest account in the portfolio — twice the base rate, and still more likely to renew than not. Internalising that sentence is most of what separates a useful programme from a panicked one.

The presentation transform. Most organisations ship a 0–100 score rather than a probability, via a monotone transform: points proportional to each coefficient, rebased so the portfolio spans the range. This preserves ranking exactly and destroys calibration entirely — a score of 38 has no interpretation, and nobody can say what fraction of 38s churn. That is acceptable only if the score is used for ordering, which is what Sneha needed. If finance then multiplies score by ARR to forecast renewal revenue, the transform has silently corrupted the forecast — the commonest invisible defect in mature programmes.

Calibration and lift, separately. Discrimination asks whether the model ranks correctly; calibration asks whether its stated probabilities are true. A model can rank perfectly and be uniformly twice too pessimistic. Vikram checked calibration by decile rather than in aggregate, because aggregate calibration hides compensating errors at the ends.

The confounded coefficient. The executive-contact term is protective, and it is the one feature an expert would refuse to act on. Executives call accounts they have been told matter, and accounts they enjoy talking to; the association runs both ways. Telling the field to make more executive calls to move the score is a textbook Goodhart failure — the feature was a marker, not a cause, and forcing it breaks the association that made it useful. Vikram kept it in the model for prediction and stripped it from the reason codes shown to CSMs, a division most teams never make.

4. When it applies, and when it is actively misleading

The conditions can be stated as claims checkable in an afternoon.

ConditionDastak SystemsElaan Cloud
C1. Churn is decided by identifiable people over an observable periodYes — a committee meets 6–10 weeks before expiryPartly — a third are silent card failures
C2. Enough events to learn from (roughly 40+ in the training window)Yes — 63 eventsYes — 380 events
C3. Account-level instrumentation mapping to delivered valueMostly — two on-premise deployments send no telemetryYes — fully hosted
C4. Capacity to treat a flagged account differentlyYes — 60 save-plays a quarter, 410 accountsNo — four people, 3,100 workspaces
C5. The churn is saveable by something the vendor controlsMostly — except forced consolidation after insurer M&AYes, but the intervention is an email

C4 is the condition practitioners skip, and it decides the shape of the answer. A score is an attention-allocation instrument; where there is no discretionary attention to allocate, the right output is an automated intervention rule, and precision matters far less than the cost of being wrong. Elaan failed C4 outright, which is why Rohan's instinct to stop having a score was not laziness.

Three situations make scores actively misleading rather than merely weak. Exogenous churn: when an insurer is acquired and consolidates onto the acquirer's platform, the account was lost in a boardroom the vendor was not in, and a red flag creates the illusion of a preventable failure. Seasonal products: a statutory-filing module whose usage collapses every May is behaving as designed, and a usage-weighted score raises an annual false alarm that trains the team to ignore it. Post-intervention data: once a save programme runs, red accounts get help and renew, so apparent accuracy degrades because the programme works. Without an untreated holdout you cannot tell a decayed model from a successful one.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product. Dastak sold adjudication and network management on one contract. An account can be delighted with one and abandoning the other, and a composite averages them into a serene amber. Mature practice is a score per product plus a roll-up taking the minimum rather than the mean where products are separately cancellable, because the risk is disjunctive.

Two-sided marketplaces. Two populations, different churn physics, asymmetric counts; a blended score is dominated by whichever side carries the revenue weighting, and the other side dies invisibly. Section 8 works this through at Farmaish Bazaar.

Regulated and on-premise deployments. Two of Dastak's insurer customers ran in their own data centres under contractual bars on telemetry egress — among its largest accounts and its least observable. Mature companies handle this by running a parallel, honestly-labelled qualitative score for that segment and refusing to put both on the same axis in a board chart.

Hardware plus software. Damini Power Systems, shipping battery-telemetry hardware with a monitoring subscription, found device heartbeats both an excellent and a terrible input: a dead sensor looks identical to an abandoned deployment. The disambiguating feature was replacement-part order cadence, which lived in the ERP, not the analytics stack.

AI-native products. At Ekagra AI, consumption in tokens and agent runs rose sharply in the two months before churn at several accounts — users were retrying failing tasks. Volume and value diverged; the useful feature was the task-completion ratio, runs ending in an accepted output over runs started. Any AI product billing on consumption should assume its headline usage metric is contaminated by failure retries until proven otherwise.

The seams. The most consequential edge case is organisational. Product owns instrumentation; customer success owns the score; sales owns the renewal and overrides the score with relationship conviction; finance forecasts from a different model entirely. Mature companies say they reconcile these. The better ones nominate one as the system of record and require the others to log disagreement with a reason — which over four quarters produces the only genuinely useful dataset in the building: a record of whose overrides were right.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

An expert reads the vector, not the scalar. Composition hides compensating movements: usage climbing while sponsorship collapses nets out to a flat score. The tell is a score unmoved for three periods while its inputs have moved a great deal; the obvious reading, stability, is exactly wrong. Experts keep input variance visible beside the composite.

Velocity beats level. Most churn comes from accounts that fell, not accounts that sit low. An account at 45 for two years is at 45 because of how it uses the product; one that went from 82 to 61 in six weeks is undergoing something. The tell is a red bucket holding the same names every quarter — the programme is measuring account character, not risk.

Lead time is a feature property, not a model property. Two models with identical discrimination are worth different amounts depending on whether their power comes from features that move ninety days out or nine. The tell is a top feature like ticket volume in the last fortnight: accurate, and too late to use.

Base rates govern what the score can mean. At a 15 per cent base rate, a red bucket churning at 46 per cent is a threefold lift and still wrong more often than right. The tell is anyone calling the score “85 per cent accurate” — a figure achievable by predicting nobody ever churns.

Anything a field team can write to will be written to. Within a quarter of Dastak publishing its weights, the distribution of “executive contact in last 60 days” developed a spike at day 58. The tell is a feature distribution with a cliff at a threshold; the fix is to prefer features from systems the field does not control — calendars, product logs, billing — accepting slightly worse discrimination for durability.

Denominators move for happy reasons. Usage ratios have seats underneath them, and seats grow when customers expand. Elaan's July red wave was 340 workspaces that had just bought licences, depressing the active-seat ratio. The tell is risk flags clustering a month after upsell. Experts add a grace window after any seat change and model seat growth as its own feature, where it usually carries a protective coefficient.

Intervention destroys the evidence. Once the programme acts on the score, outcomes for flagged accounts are no longer the counterfactual and every later validation is confounded. The tell is measured performance falling each quarter while the renewal rate improves. The only clean remedy is an untreated holdout, which everyone endorses and almost nobody maintains, because deliberately not saving accounts you believe are at risk is hard to defend in a quarterly review.

The dangerous bucket is amber. Red accounts get escalated and green ones left alone; amber has no owner and no protocol. The tell is a logged-activity count lower for amber than for either neighbour. Failing programmes rarely fail at the model; they fail because the middle third of the portfolio has a colour and no consequence attached to it.

7. How this changes across product types and stages

In consumer products the construct largely does not apply: there is no account and no one to call, and the equivalent discipline is cohort retention analysis where the intervention is a product change. In B2B mid-market it is at its most useful, accounts being numerous enough to model and valuable enough to warrant individual attention — Dastak exactly. In enterprise the predictive contribution falls and the coordinating one rises: with forty accounts no model is worth fitting, and the score's job is to force a structured quarterly conversation about each named relationship. Marketplaces need separate scores per side, always. In hardware-plus-software the supply chain carries signal the software never sees. In AI products consumption needs a quality denominator before it means anything.

Stage changes the honest answer more than most admit. Below roughly fifty churn events a fitted model is noise wearing a lab coat, and the defensible instrument is three or four transparently weighted signals reviewed monthly and labelled provisional. Between fifty and a few hundred events, regression-derived weights become defensible and segmentation necessary. Above that the problems stop being statistical and become organisational: who owns the number, what happens when sales disagrees, and whether anyone still measures lead time.

8. Three worked examples

Dastak Systems: ranking under a capacity constraint

Sneha could run sixty save-plays a quarter; the question is what that buys. Sorting 410 accounts by predicted risk into deciles of 41 gave the distribution below.

DecileAccountsChurn eventsRateLift vs 15.4% baseCumulative % of churn captured
D10 (riskiest)411946.3%3.0×30%
D9411229.3%1.9×49%
D841922.0%1.4×63%
D7–D51231512.2%0.8×87%
D4–D116484.9%0.3×100%

Sixty save-plays covers D10 and most of D9: 82 accounts holding 31 of 63 expected events, at an average top-decile ARR of ₹34 lakh. If a save-play converts one in four would-be departures — optimistic but not absurd ten weeks out — the programme retains roughly eight accounts, about ₹2.4 crore of ARR. The same sixty engagements spread at random would sit on nine expected events and retain two. That four-to-one ratio is the entire economic case, and it does not require the score to be right about any individual account.

Elaan Cloud: when the score is accurate and useless

Tanvi's model had an AUC of 0.81, better than Dastak's 0.76, and still produced the July disaster: 340 red workspaces, 96 per cent of which renewed. The mechanical fault was the seat denominator; expansion depressed the active-seat ratio and the model had no seat-growth feature to offset it. The structural fault was worse. Elaan's only interventions were a lifecycle email and an in-product banner, both unconditionally cheap. When intervention costs nothing, the optimal precision of the trigger is low: flag generously, because a false positive costs one ignored email. The score had been tuned as though attention were scarce, in an organisation where it was free but nearly powerless.

Farmaish Bazaar: the blended score that hid a collapse

Farmaish Bazaar ran a freight marketplace matching 1,850 shipper accounts with 6,400 fleet owners, taking four per cent of ₹610 crore of annual booked freight. Its health score was a single composite weighted by GMV contribution, so forty large shippers effectively determined the portfolio number. Through the second and third quarters of FY26 it held between 69 and 72, comfortably green. Underneath, 1,100 fleet owners went inactive, median load-acceptance time rose from 11 minutes to 29, and three large shippers left in one month citing fulfilment reliability — ₹2.4 crore of annualised revenue. The score had not failed to notice supply-side decay; it had been built so that supply-side decay could not move it.

The recovery is instructive because it was not a modelling fix. Farmaish split the score in two: supply health on loads accepted over loads offered plus payment-cycle days, demand health on fill rate and time-to-first-truck. It moved supply-score ownership to the regional supply managers, who had budget for driver-payment acceleration. And it held 300 randomly chosen supply accounts out of intervention for two quarters, so the effect could be measured rather than asserted. Supply-side annual churn fell from 31 per cent to 19 over nine months; the holdout attributed about seven of those twelve points to the intervention, the rest to an unrelated payment-terms change. Without it the team would have claimed all twelve.

9. Failure modes, their early warning, and the cost of lateness

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Features chosen for availability, not lead timeTop features are support and billing eventsWhat is each feature's median lead time?A renewal cycle of alerts too late to act on
Score read as a probability after a monotone transformFinance multiplies score by ARRWhat fraction of accounts scoring 60 churned?A forecast miss whose cause stays invisible for two quarters
Field gaming of self-reported inputsDistribution spike just inside a thresholdWhich inputs can a CSM edit?Silent decay; trust is lost once and not regained
No untreated holdoutAUC falls as renewal rate risesWhat happens to red accounts we do not touch?Years of spend with no attributable effect
One score across segments or marketplace sidesBucket distribution nearly identical across segmentsDoes red churn at different rates by segment?A whole population's collapse arrives as a surprise
Amber with no protocolFewer logged touches on amber than red or greenFor the last ten ambers, who acted and when?Steady leakage across most of the portfolio
Onboarding accounts scored on the mature curveNew accounts cluster at the extremesAre accounts under ninety days scored separately?Alarm fatigue that trains the team to dismiss red

None of these is a statistical failure. Every one is a failure to specify what the number means, who owns it and what happens when it moves — which is why programmes led purely by data science fail more often than those led jointly with the field.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether the composite should exist at all. The disaggregationist case is stronger than its reception suggests: composition is lossy, every weight asserts a substitutability nobody believes (is one lost module worth eighteen points of seat ratio?), and the scalar invites executives to manage the number. Its evidence is that action follows reason codes, not scores. It would be wrong if organisations could hold six independent signals in mind across 400 accounts, which the operational school's evidence — unaggregated dashboards get ignored — suggests they cannot.

Interpretable models versus accurate ones. The actuarial position is that a boosted model at 0.84 AUC saves more accounts than a logistic one at 0.76, and that reason codes can be reconstructed post hoc. The operational counter is that a CSM who cannot explain why an account is red will not defend the call against a sales director, so the accuracy never converts into action. The disagreement is empirical and almost never tested; it stays open because hardly anyone runs the holdout that would settle it.

Whether usage can stand in for value. The value-realisation school points to a real class of accounts: heavy usage, no realised outcome, churn when a new CFO asks what the line item bought. The counter is that outcome data is self-reported, sparse, and gathered by the same CSMs whose performance it reflects, making it systematically optimistic. Both are right about the other's weakness; the honest practice is to carry the outcome measure separately and never average it into the usage composite.

Whether scores should be shown to the customer. A minority practice shares the score with the customer's sponsor, arguing that it converts a surveillance instrument into a shared plan and surfaces the vendor's blind spots. The objection is that it becomes a negotiating position at renewal. There is no good public evidence either way, and the answer probably turns on whether the sponsor's incentives align with the vendor's.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds the score. Someone who has internalised it starts from the intervention and works backwards: what would we do differently, who would do it, how many can they do, how much lead time do they need? Those questions fix the tolerable false-positive rate and whether a model is warranted at all. The mastered practitioner quotes the base rate unprompted, distinguishes ranking from probability without being asked, defends a holdout on the grounds that an unmeasurable programme cannot be funded, retires features that stop earning their lead time, publishes the misses beside the hits, and will say plainly that an account's score is uninformative because the account is unobservable. Above all, they treat the score as a claim that can be wrong in a specified way, not a summary of how things are going.

12. What each protagonist decided

Aparna Rege shipped the model as a ranked queue with three reason codes per account, not a number on a dashboard. She refused to let it appear in the board pack as a portfolio average, since a monotone-transformed score has no aggregate meaning; the board saw expected renewal revenue with a range instead. She removed the two self-reported fields, accepting a drop in AUC from 0.79 to 0.76, and held fifteen per cent of D9 and D10 accounts out of the save programme for two quarters over Sneha's objection, so that by March 2027 the team would know what the programme was worth. Rohan Pillai decided the opposite way, for defensible reasons: he retired Elaan's composite for three threshold rules — activation stall, sole-admin dependency, integration disconnection — each with a named owner in Imran's team and an automated first action. At ₹1.3 lakh of ACV the question was never which workspaces were at risk, but which could be helped by something that costs nothing.

Discussion questions. First: Vikram's model gains accuracy from a feature nobody should act on and loses accuracy when the field can edit its inputs. On what principle should a team decide which features belong in a model people will act on? Second: Aparna's holdout means knowingly not helping roughly a dozen at-risk accounts for two quarters. Is that defensible, and if so, to whom must it be defended beforehand rather than after? Third: Farmaish Bazaar's blended score was built by competent people making a reasonable weighting choice. What design-time review step would have caught it — and would that step have caught Elaan's seat-denominator fault too?

13. Going deeper

  1. B2B product metrics — the raw material a score aggregates; without account-level usage and breadth data there is nothing to compose.
  2. Renewals, churn and NRR — the outcome the score is judged against, and the arithmetic converting saves into retained revenue.
  3. Customer success metrics and the PM — how the score becomes an operating cadence with owners rather than a dashboard.
  4. What makes a good metric — which candidate inputs deserve a weight and which are merely convenient.
  5. Vanity vs actionable metrics — separating lead-time-bearing features from ones that merely correlate.
  6. GAME framework — tying each metric to the goal, action and evaluation it serves.
  7. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — where retention work sits relative to the other two, and what trades against it.
  8. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — the source of the seat-denominator fault and why ratios mislead.
  9. North Star metric — whether a composite belongs at the top of a company at all: section 10's argument, one level up.

— Reading page prepared for the ISB Product Management knowledge graph.

Alaap Systems: The Night Before the Review

Bengaluru, 15 November 2026. Rukmini Deshpande has four exhibits that disagree with one another, a board that wants a number, and a suspicion that the question she has been asked is not the question that matters.

1. Sunday night

The Diwali lights were still up along Bannerghatta Road on the evening of Sunday, 15 November 2026, a week after the festival, when Rukmini Deshpande sat down in the empty fifth floor of Alaap Systems' office with four printed exhibits and a marker pen. At half past eleven she had arranged them on the table in a row, and the row did not make sense.

The first said that Alaap's account health score was working: green accounts had renewed at 97 per cent over eight quarters, red at 68. The second said that the company's net revenue retention, measured properly, was 91 per cent — that is, the existing customer base was shrinking. The third said that fourteen of the top forty accounts had begun sending some portion of their traffic through a second vendor, but carried a footnote about a purchased industry panel and a margin of error wide enough to drive a lorry through. The fourth said that 38 per cent of accounts had no usable platform telemetry at all.

At eleven the next morning, Rukmini would stand in front of the leadership team and the two investor directors who sat on Alaap's board and propose what the company should do about retention before Series D diligence opened in January. Jaideep Rathore, the chief executive, had asked her for "a health score we can actually trust, and a number for the January deck." She had begun the weekend intending to produce exactly that. She was ending it unsure whether the score was the problem at all.

2. How Alaap got here

Alaap Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by Jaideep Rathore and two engineers from a telecom messaging aggregator, on a simple observation: every Indian bank, lender, insurer, retailer and logistics company had to send billions of messages a year — one-time passwords, delivery updates, payment confirmations, policy renewals, offers — and almost all of them did it through pipes they did not control, with tooling they disliked. Alaap built the pipes and the tooling together: a high-throughput messaging gateway connected to every Indian telecom operator, plus a software console on top for campaigns, customer journeys, segmentation, template management and delivery analytics.

By November 2026 the company handled roughly 41 billion messages a year for 890 enterprise accounts across SMS, WhatsApp Business messaging, RCS, voice and push. Gross revenue for the year to March 2026 was ₹640 crore. Net revenue — what remained after paying telecom operators and platform providers for termination and conversation fees — was ₹118 crore. The top twenty-five accounts produced 61 per cent of net revenue. Customers included private banks, non-banking financial companies, two large insurers, a dozen fintechs, several direct-to-consumer brands of the kind that had grown up alongside Nykaa and boAt, and quick-commerce and logistics firms whose delivery notifications ran through Alaap's gateway around the clock.

One decision from 2023 shaped everything that followed. In March of that year, facing aggressive pricing from established aggregators and from the in-house teams at large banks, Alaap launched what it called Platform Zero: the software console — journeys, segments, analytics, template governance, the whole thing — would be free to any customer committing a minimum annual message volume. The console had previously been sold at ₹18 to ₹45 lakh a year depending on seats and modules. After Platform Zero, it had no price at all.

The strategy worked commercially and beautifully. Alaap took share; gross revenue tripled in three years. But it had three consequences that nobody had modelled at the time. Customer contracts became volume-commitment contracts with thirty-day termination for convenience, because that is how messaging is bought. The console, having no price, acquired no procurement scrutiny, no implementation budget on the customer's side and no separate renewal conversation. And internally, because the console generated no revenue line, nobody was accountable for its adoption. Aravind Pillai's platform team in Pune instrumented the console's events in 2023 as a side project during a release, and the instrumentation had never been validated.

3. The industry around it

The market Alaap operated in was shaped by regulation to an unusual degree. Commercial messaging in India runs on the TRAI-mandated distributed-ledger registration framework, under which every sender identity, template and consent record must be registered and scrubbed before delivery; enforcement had tightened steadily, and each tightening produced a step change in delivered volumes that had nothing to do with any customer's satisfaction. The Reserve Bank of India's authentication requirements governed the one-time-password traffic that formed Alaap's most reliable volume. Customers in lending and insurance answered to the RBI and IRDAI respectively for what they could say in a message; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act governed what Alaap itself could retain, and expressly limited what Alaap could look at inside message content, which cut off an entire category of signal that a vendor might otherwise have used to judge how a customer was doing.

Economics shifted too. When the WhatsApp Business platform moved its pricing from a per-conversation to a per-message basis during 2025, every large customer of every Indian CPaaS vendor re-examined its messaging mix; many cut promotional volume sharply and moved traffic back to SMS or to their own app's push notifications. Volumes across the industry fell for a quarter and then recomposed. Alaap's biggest customers were themselves under pressure from their own economics: fintechs watching unit costs after the tightening of digital-lending norms, quick-commerce firms in a fierce expansion race, and exporters and retailers adjusting to ONDC-driven changes in how orders reached them.

Alaap's global exposure ran through two doors. Rohan Mehra's team in Jersey City sold to United States-domiciled fintechs and remittance companies serving the Indian diaspora, where the messaging was cross-border and the margins were better. And the single largest account in the book was Rawnaq Retail Group FZ-LLC, a Dubai-headquartered retail and grocery group with operations across the Gulf and a sourcing arm in Mumbai, worth ₹9.4 crore of gross revenue and ₹2.1 crore of net revenue in the previous financial year.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The health score had been built in January 2025 by Farida Qureshi's customer-success organisation in Singapore, with help from Nikhil Ranade in Toronto. Its three components were message volume trend against the account's own trailing quarter (50 per cent), support ticket severity-weighted count, inverted (25 per cent), and a customer-success manager's quarterly relationship rating (25 per cent). It was validated against logo churn, and on that basis it worked: Exhibit 2 below still shows it working.

In October 2025 the score broke in a way nobody had anticipated. Following the WhatsApp pricing change, volumes fell at 60 per cent of accounts within six weeks. The volume-trend component dragged the entire book towards amber; Farida's team found itself with 340 accounts flagged and six people to work them, and the customer-success bonus pool — calculated on the share of net revenue sitting in green accounts — collapsed. In November 2025 a working group reduced the weight on volume trend from 50 per cent to 20 per cent and raised the relationship rating to 45 per cent. The book returned to green within two reporting cycles. The revision had been documented in a single slide and approved in a fortnightly operations meeting.

In February 2026 a further tightening of sender-identity scrubbing removed roughly 4 per cent of delivered volume across the book. In June 2026, the board pack reported net revenue retention of 104 per cent, which was the headline Jaideep carried into early Series D conversations. In August, preparing a cohort analysis for diligence, Nikhil rebuilt the retention calculation from the ledger rather than from the CRM and found that the 104 per cent figure had been computed on gross revenue including telecom pass-through. On net revenue the same cohort came to 91 per cent. The difference was almost entirely explained by two accounts — Rawnaq in Dubai and a quick-commerce customer in Gurugram — whose volume had grown enormously at contract rates so thin that the incremental net revenue was close to nil, while thirty-one mid-market accounts had quietly reduced their commitments.

In September, Nikhil bought access to an industry traffic panel that estimates, from sender-identity registrations and delivery-report sampling, how each large enterprise's messaging is distributed across vendors. It suggested that fourteen of Alaap's top forty accounts had added a second vendor during 2026. None of the fourteen had churned. None had reduced its contracted commitment below the minimum. Several were green.

Then came Diwali. On the night of 8 November 2026, during the single largest messaging window of the Indian year, delivery latency on one operator route rose sharply for about ninety minutes, affecting three large accounts including Rawnaq's Gulf promotional campaign. Aravind's team in Pune attributed it to operator-side congestion; the operator's own report attributed it to a retry storm from Alaap's gateway. The two accounts of the incident had not been reconciled by 15 November. What Rukmini did know was that Hiba Rahman, Rawnaq's head of customer engagement, had written to Rohan on 10 November asking for a commercial review "in light of recent performance and of the alternatives we are now evaluating."

5. The people

Rukmini Deshpande, 41, VP product, Bengaluru. Joined in 2021 from a payments company. Owns the console and, since June, the health-score programme. Her stated position is that the score must be rebuilt on platform adoption rather than volume. What she has not said to anyone is that she pushed for Platform Zero in 2023 and believes it may have been the mistake that created this situation — an admission that would be awkward eight weeks before diligence.

Jaideep Rathore, 46, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants a clean retention story for Series D and has told the board that the 104 per cent figure was "a definitional matter now corrected." His position is that the health score should be simplified, not rebuilt, and that the company's real problem is that the console is not good enough to be worth paying for. His incentive is a raise at a valuation that a 91 per cent net retention figure would materially reduce. He has not told the leadership team that one investor has already asked for a cohort file.

Farida Qureshi, 39, VP customer success, Singapore. Built the original score and defends the November 2025 reweighting as the only way to keep her team functioning. Her position is that the relationship rating is the most valuable signal Alaap has, because her managers know things no telemetry can see. Her team's bonus is calculated on net revenue in green accounts. What she is not saying is that she has privately concluded that two of the fourteen dual-sourcing accounts are already lost and has been managing expectations rather than escalating.

Nikhil Ranade, 34, head of revenue operations and analytics, Toronto. Found the retention discrepancy and bought the panel. His position is that the score should be re-labelled: predict net revenue erosion over the next two quarters, not logo churn. What he is not saying loudly enough is that the panel's per-account share estimates carry a confidence interval of roughly ±15 percentage points, that its coverage of WhatsApp traffic is poor, and that for nine of the fourteen flagged accounts the finding rests on a single quarter of sampling.

Aravind Pillai, 36, engineering lead, platform, Pune. Owns the console and the event pipeline. His position is that no score built on console telemetry can be trusted until the pipeline is rebuilt, which he estimates at seven weeks. What he is not saying is that he deprioritised that rebuild twice during 2026 in order to ship a Diwali campaign-scheduling feature that Rohan's team had promised to two accounts, and that the double-counting of message retries in the console's own delivery analytics may have contributed to what customers saw on 8 November.

Rohan Mehra, 48, senior vice-president of sales, Jersey City. Position: this is a pricing and service problem, not a measurement problem, and the answer is a loyalty rate card for accounts that consolidate volume with Alaap. His commission plan is written on gross revenue. He is not saying that he has already indicated to Hiba Rahman that a rate reduction is possible.

Lena Brückner, 33, design lead, Berlin. Position: the console is not adopted because it is genuinely hard to use — her team's study found that building a two-step journey took a median of 47 minutes and that four of six participants abandoned. She is not saying that the study had six participants, all from mid-market accounts, and none from the banks that generate most of the volume.

Meenakshi Subramanian, 52, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. Position: eleven of the top forty accounts are gross-margin negative after support cost, and the company should raise their prices and accept the churn. She is not saying that three of those eleven are the reference accounts named in the Series D deck.

6. Exhibits

8. The options as Rukmini currently sees them

Option one: rebuild the score on console adoption. Replace volume trend and the relationship rating with breadth of console use — journeys live, segments saved, template governance adopted, delivery analytics consumed — normalised per account. This is the design Rukmini believes in, and it is the design that would have caught the mid-market erosion. It also requires Aravind's seven weeks, cannot see 38 per cent of accounts at all, and would mark the two largest growth accounts red on the strength of a metric the customer has never been asked to care about, for a product Alaap gives away.

Option two: change the label. Keep a model but train it to predict two-quarter net revenue erosion rather than logo churn, using the panel's share-of-wallet estimates as a feature and as a partial label. This is Nikhil's proposal and it targets the thing that is actually happening. It rests on data with a ±15-point confidence interval bought from a third party, it would put a purchased estimate into a number that reaches the board, and it cannot be validated against anything Alaap owns.

Option three: stop scoring the top forty. Run the top forty accounts through a structured quarterly review — named economic buyer, documented value hypothesis in rupees, evidence of console use or a reason for its absence, explicit question about second vendors — and keep a simple score only for the 850-account tail, where attention must be rationed and where logo churn is the real risk. This is cheap and honest. It also produces no forecast for January, which is what Jaideep has asked for, and it depends on customer-success managers asking customers directly about competitors, which Farida's team has historically avoided.

Rukmini had written all three on the whiteboard and then, at a quarter to midnight, written a fourth line underneath and left it there: "Or: the console has no price, so nobody defends it, so nothing we measure about it predicts anything. Is this a measurement problem at all?" Beneath that she had added: "And what is the unit? The account, or the use case? Account 3 is loyal on OTP and gone on marketing. One score cannot hold both."

9. The deadline and the constraints

The leadership review is at eleven on Monday, 16 November. Series D diligence opens in the second week of January, and the investor who asked for a cohort file will receive whatever definition of retention the company settles on. Alaap's board has approved ₹1.4 crore for data and analytics work in the current year, of which ₹62 lakh remains; the panel subscription costs ₹34 lakh a year to renew in February. There is a hiring freeze on non-engineering roles until April. Aravind has fourteen engineers and a committed roadmap through January that includes an RCS capability two banks have been promised. Customer contracts carry thirty-day termination for convenience, so any account can reduce or stop volume within a month, and the console cannot be withdrawn from a customer without renegotiating the volume commitment it was bundled into. Under the DPDP Act and Alaap's own contracts, message content is off limits as a source of signal; only metadata, delivery status and console events may be used. And Rawnaq's commercial review, whatever it turns out to be, will be conducted in December.

At ten past midnight Rukmini turned the four exhibits face down, one after another, and then turned the third one back over. The panel estimate for Rawnaq read 70 per cent, plus or minus fifteen. If it was 85, the account was fine and Hiba's email was a negotiation. If it was 55, the largest customer in the book had already moved a third of its traffic and nobody at Alaap had known for a year. The health score, refreshed that morning, read 81. The lights along Bannerghatta Road went off at half past twelve, and she was still there.
